amendments.rule: An English function word the ASV supplies for an adverbial accusative belongs to the noun whose case-function licenses it — *as a bird*, *to your mountain* — and is never `added`. **An appositional or measure nominal the ASV introduces with a supplied preposition is read the same way.** Where a noun or numeral stands in the clause with no preposition and no object marker on it, and the ASV writes an *of* or a *for* before it to state what that nominal contributes, the word is that nominal's own rendering: `אֹרֶךְ חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` → *the length ... of five and twenty thousand*, `תֹּכֶן אֶחָד` → *of one measure*, `לַאֲחֻזָּה עֶשְׂרִים לְשָׁכֹת` → *for a possession ..., for twenty chambers*, `חַטָּאת שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *a he goat ... for a sin offering*. It goes to the word it stands before, which is the noun or numeral opening that phrase, and the unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme under rules 24 and 31; the supplied preposition is never the head. **Read *an *of* or a *for** as any preposition the ASV writes for the nominal's own contribution, and not as a closed list.** What licenses the word is that a bare nominal stands in the clause and the English needs a word to say what it contributes there, so read the condition and not the lemma, exactly as rule 40 does for the preposition it silences: a comparative *as* before a nominal the ASV construes as a comparison — `פַּלְגֵי מַיִם` → ***as*** *the watercourses* — an agent *by* before a bare nominal the ASV construes with a passive participle — `מְבַקְשֵׁי מָוֶת` → *driven to and fro* ***by*** *them that seek death* — and a *with* or an *in* before a nominal standing in a `מִן` comparison — `אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים` → ***with*** *a contentious woman*, `בֵּית חָבֶר` → ***in*** *a wide house* — all go to the nominal on the same terms as an *of* or a *for*, and this rule's first sentence already writes *as* and *to* for the adverbial accusative. Three limits, each stated where it belongs. A word an object marker stands to take is the marker's under rule 16, and an *as for* the ASV writes before a topicalized phrase no marker and no preposition stands on is `added` under that rule rather than this one, since a nominal's fronting is not a case-function. A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own bare object is the verb's under rule 44, and this rule's own closing paragraph disposes of one a predicate's valency needs. And a coordinating or subordinating connective the ASV writes beside such a phrase is not a word spent on the nominal at all: rules 14 and 55 count those against the morphemes that could carry them. **A preposition standing elsewhere in the clause that has already taken an English word of its own does not make such a word a surplus.** Rule 52's count governs two English words offered to one morpheme, and here each phrase has a rendering of its own, so a written `לְ` rendered *for a possession* does not silence the *for* the ASV writes before the phrase standing beside it. **But an English preposition the ASV writes again over a member the Hebrew coordinates under one written preposition is that preposition's, and not the bare nominal's.** Hebrew gaps a preposition in the later members of a coordination where English rewrites it, and the word the ASV writes there is the distributed scope of the one written morpheme: it joins that morpheme's possibly discontinuous unit under rule 25, however much stands between and whatever word the ASV chose for the members in between. `בְּכֹל מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה וַאֲשֶׁר הָיוּ לְפָנָיו` → *among all the kings of Judah, nor* ***among*** *them that were before him* gives the second *among* to the one `בְּ`, and `בַּחְלַח וּבְחָבוֹר נְהַר גּוֹזָן וְעָרֵי מָדָי` → *in Halah and on the Habor the river of Gozan and* ***in*** *the cities of the Medes* gives the third preposition to the first `בְּ`, across the second member's own `בְּ` holding the *on* written for it. What tells this from the preceding sentences is order and repetition together, not that the nominal is bare: this sentence governs a member coordinated after a written preposition of its own phrase whose English the ASV has simply written again, and the earlier sentences govern a nominal standing before any such preposition, or in a phrase where none is written at all. So read whether a preposition of that phrase stands earlier in the coordination before giving the word to the noun — `הַנִּמְצָא בֵית־יְהוָה וּבְאֹצְרוֹת בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ` → *that was found* ***in*** *the house of Jehovah, and in the treasures of the king's house* leaves its first *in* to `בַּיִת` under this rule's first sentence, because the written `בְּ` stands after it and nothing is being repeated. Test by subtraction as elsewhere: ask whether the English word states what a bare nominal contributes to its clause, or restates a relation a written preposition already carries over that member. **But the noun must be present.** Where the ASV supplies the head noun as well as the function word, no morpheme is there to carry either, and the whole supplied phrase is its own `added` unit under rule 30: `חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת בַּחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת` → *five hundred* ***in length*** *by five hundred* ***in breadth*** supplies both the preposition and the dimension noun in a clause whose Hebrew names neither, exactly as the italic ***reeds*** of `חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` supplies a measure noun. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English and ask whether a Hebrew noun standing in the clause has lost the relation it bears, or whether what has gone is a noun the Hebrew never wrote. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7. **And a bare noun that completes a predicate's own valency is not an adverbial accusative at all.** Where a verb or a predicate adjective governs a bare noun as its complement — no preposition and no object marker on it — and the English predicate can reach that complement only through a preposition the ASV has written, that word answers to the predicate's valency and joins the predicate's unit under rule 44, while the noun keeps its own English: `מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full* ***of*** *the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full* ***of*** *fatness* both give the *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave `דִין` and `דֶשֶׁן` their own words. Decide it by asking whether the ASV had a relation to choose: where the English predicate admits no other word before such a complement — *full of* is the only way English writes it — the preposition is the predicate's, and where the word states what the noun contributes to the clause and another would have served, this rule governs and the word is the noun's, as it does for `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil* ***in*** *rain* and `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty* ***in*** *strength*. Read the English predicate rather than where the noun stands, since Hebrew writes such a complement before its predicate as readily as after it, and JOB.36.16 and JOB.36.17 are the two shapes in one chapter.
amendments.why: Rule 33 as written says a supplied function word before a bare nominal belongs to that nominal and is never `added`, and its three limits name only an object marker, a verb's valency and a connective. It does not say what happens when the bare nominal is a later member of a coordination whose preposition the Hebrew writes once and the ASV writes again, which is the shape 2KI.18.5 and 18.11 present. Rule 25's distributed-scope sentence already decides that case and cites `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁעַ` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging*, but a reader arriving from rule 33 has no reason to check it, and rule 33's over-broad first sentence is what they would apply. The added limit narrows rule 33 where it stands, states the discriminator as order plus repetition rather than the bareness of the noun, and keeps the ordinary case explicit with 18.15, where the bare nominal precedes the phrase's written preposition and the supplied *in* is the noun's. No corpus row contradicts it: rule 25's own precedent is the same construction, and the chapter's other supplied prepositions before bare nominals (17, 26, 28, 37) are unaffected because no written preposition of their phrases precedes them.

conventions: רַב־שָׁקֵה is one fused unit rendered *Rabshakeh* at every occurrence (17, 19, 26, 27, 28, 37), headed on רַב; the coordinate title רַב־סָרִיס standing beside it in 17 is split, because the ASV writes *Rab saris* in two words. The shared רַב is not evidence either way: the ASV's word count decides each title on its own under rule 30.

In the title הַמֶּלֶךְ חִזְקִיָּהוּ the article is `unrepresented` throughout (9, 13, 17), because the ASV writes *king Hezekiah* with no determiner; the noun keeps only its own word and nothing is supplied for the article.

A gentilic adverbial of language takes the supplied *in the* and the supplied generic noun *language* into its own unit, headed on the gentilic: אֲרָמִית → *in the Syrian language* and יְהוּדִית → *in the Jews language* (26 twice, 28). Neither the preposition nor the generic is `added`, and neither is the head.

Where the ASV rewrites a preposition over a member the Hebrew coordinates under one written preposition, the repetition belongs to that written morpheme and its unit is discontinuous: בְּכֹל מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה וַאֲשֶׁר הָיוּ לְפָנָיו → *among ... nor among* (5), and בַּחְלַח וּבְחָבוֹר ... וְעָרֵי מָדָי → *in ... on ... in* (11), where the second *in* is the first בְּ's across the second member's own *on*. Where instead the bare nominal stands before any written preposition of its phrase, or none is written, the supplied word is the nominal's under rule 33: בֵית־יְהוָה → *in the house* (15), the two bare accusatives of Jerusalem (17), the language adverbials (26, 28), and קְרוּעֵי בְגָדִים → *with ... rent* (37).

Where the ASV compresses a construct chain into a single English noun that writes only one member's lexeme, that member takes the word and the other is `unrepresented` rather than fused: מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם → *their own water* leaves רֶגֶל nothing (27), and אֶרֶץ זֵית יִצְהָר → *a land of olive trees* leaves יִצְהָר nothing (32). Rule 30's one-rendering condition is unmet in both, because the English noun is a word the ASV spends on the other morpheme in particular. BSB represents both; the disagreement was reviewed and is a convention difference.

report: Read all 37 verses end to end against the candidate table. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source licensing the difference, so no patches and no re-validation.

Checked in full: the הָיָה presentative frames (1, 9) both keep their complementizer, because neither apodosis writes a waw the ASV renders. The numeral-plus-שָׁנָה date formula (1, 9, 10, 13) always gives a supplied determiner to the noun and a written article the *the*. The title in 9, 13 and 17 always leaves the article `unrepresented` for a bare *king Hezekiah*. רַב־שָׁקֵה fuses at all six occurrences while רַב־סָרִיס in the same verse splits, which is the ASV's word count and not two analyses of one shape. The language adverbials (26 twice, 28) are identical. The אִישׁ distributives (31 three times, 33) differ only in the English written. Every supplied object pronoun or noun is `added` (12 twice, 15, 16, 26), none folded into a neighbouring verb.

The one candidate that looked like a split is the supplied preposition before a bare nominal: 18.11 gives a third *in* to the written בְּ as distributed scope, while 18.15 gives a first *in* to בֵית under rule 33. The difference is source-licensed and holds chapter-wide. Where a written preposition of the same phrase stands earlier in the coordination and the ASV writes its English again (5 *among ... among*, 11 *in ... in*), the repetition is that morpheme's under rule 25; where the bare nominal stands before any written preposition of its phrase, or none is written at all (15, 17 twice, 26 twice, 28, 37), rule 33 gives the word to the noun. Recorded as a convention and offered as an amendment narrowing rule 33, whose own three limits do not name this case.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The Td × 24 and R × 12 blocks are the documented supplied-determiner and recast-preposition conventions. The three waws (17, 18, 21) open clauses for which the ASV writes no connective, rule 14. The 18.21 ethical-dative suffix and the 18.22 paragogic nun are rules 40 and 32. The 18.29 object marker is rule 16. The 18.36 הִיא is the unrendered resumptive of a tripartite clause whose copula rule 20 sends to the predicate. רַגְלֵי (27) and יִצְהָר (32) are the two substantive cases: the ASV compresses each construct chain into one English noun that writes only the other member's lexeme, so rule 30's one-rendering condition is unmet and rule 2 splits, leaving one member `unrepresented`. BSB attaches both to the rendered noun; that is a convention difference, and the ASV writes nothing for them.

The two large-source-unit flags (7 unit 6 בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר → *whithersoever*, 21 unit 17 אֲשֶׁר עָלָיו → *whereon*) are genuine fusions under rules 30 and 22; each single English word carries every morpheme's sense, so neither is divisible. The chapter's ketiv/qere units in 27 are prepared decisions and neither is marked excluded, so rule 53 does not arise.
